html:
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o was a Kenyan novelist, playwright and critic, often called East Africa's leading writer. After making his name in English, he turned to writing in his mother tongue, Gikuyu, and argued that Africans must "decolonise the mind".

Born James Ngugi near Limuru, he grew up during the Mau Mau rebellion, which tore his family and village apart. He studied at Makerere, and his Weep Not, Child (1964) was the first novel in English by an East African. A Grain of Wheat (1967) and Petals of Blood (1977) looked hard at the hopes and betrayals of independent Kenya.

In 1977 he co-wrote a play in Gikuyu, performed by villagers at Kamiriithu. The government of Jomo Kenyatta banned it and held him in prison without trial for a year. There he wrote a novel in Gikuyu on toilet paper. He went into exile in 1982 under Daniel arap Moi and taught in Britain and the United States.

His essay collection Decolonising the Mind (1986) made the case for writing in African languages, and set him against writers like Chinua Achebe who chose English.
